Family Health

Genetic testing for inherited cancer risk: what a result can tell you

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A family history of cancer can leave you wondering whether the same illness is inevitable for you. Genetic testing can sometimes identify an inherited change that increases risk and helps guide screening or treatment. It cannot predict every cancer or tell you with certainty whether one will develop. The useful starting point is a discussion of your personal and family history, followed by a clear explanation of what a particular test could change.

Cancer is genetic, but it is not always inherited

Genes help control how cells grow, divide and repair damage. Cancer develops when changes disrupt these controls. Many such changes arise during life, through errors as cells divide or influences such as environmental exposures. A genetic change in a tumor does not automatically mean the person inherited it or can pass it to a child.

Hereditary cancer risk concerns a harmful change present in the germline: the genetic information that can be passed through an egg or sperm. What is inherited is a predisposition, not cancer itself. The National Cancer Institute estimates that harmful inherited changes account for about 5–10% of cancers. Cancer can also cluster in families because of shared exposures or chance, so a pattern deserves assessment rather than an automatic hereditary label.

Which cancers can have an inherited component?

Inherited variants can contribute to some breast, colorectal, prostate, ovarian and pancreatic cancers. Certain skin, thyroid and kidney cancers are also associated with hereditary syndromes. This does not mean every case of one of these cancers is hereditary, or that a single test covers them all.

Different genes are linked to different combinations and levels of risk. BRCA1 and BRCA2 are familiar examples, particularly in breast and ovarian cancer, but they are not the only relevant genes. A clinician chooses testing based on the pattern being investigated. A broad panel may be useful in some situations, while a targeted test is more informative when the family already has a confirmed harmful variant.

Inherited-risk testing and tumor testing answer different questions

Hereditary testing usually examines blood, saliva or cheek cells to look for a change that may be present throughout the body. Tumor testing examines cancer material to understand the tumor or help select treatment. The distinction is about the question being asked, not simply whether the report includes the word genetic.

A tumor result can raise suspicion of an inherited variant and prompt a separate assessment. It does not necessarily prove that the finding is inherited, and tumor testing does not replace a suitable germline test. If you have already had testing during cancer treatment, bring the actual report to a genetics appointment so the team can establish what was examined.

Begin with a personal and family risk assessment

A clinician or genetic counselor asks about your own diagnoses, ages at diagnosis, previous treatment and relevant test results. They also look at cancer in blood relatives on both sides of the family. First-degree relatives include parents, siblings and children; information about grandparents, aunts, uncles and other relatives can also reveal a pattern.

Write down the cancer type and approximate age at diagnosis where possible. Several relatives with the same cancer, related cancer types on one side of the family, more than one primary cancer in one person or unusually early diagnoses can be informative. If details are missing, say so. A small family, adoption or limited access to relatives’ records can make an apparently quiet family history less reassuring.

Who may benefit from a genetics referral?

Testing may be considered when there is a known harmful family variant, a strong pattern of related cancers, an unusually young diagnosis or a particular tumor type associated with inherited risk. A diagnosis before age 50 is one clue for some cancers, not a universal eligibility boundary. Some people qualify based on their own cancer diagnosis even without a striking family history.

For example, someone whose mother and sister had breast cancer may benefit from a genetics assessment. That does not automatically mean the correct next step is a BRCA-only test or preventive surgery. Their relatives’ ages, pathology and any previous reports help determine the approach. When possible, beginning with a relative who has had cancer can make subsequent testing of unaffected relatives more informative; if that is not possible, the team can explain the alternatives.

What genetic counseling should cover

Before testing, counseling should explain how the suspected condition can be inherited, which genes or variants the proposed test examines and what it may miss. Discuss the possible results in advance: a harmful variant, no harmful finding or a change whose significance is uncertain. Ask how each result might affect screening, treatment, reproductive decisions or relatives.

The conversation should also address your expectations, worries and practical circumstances. Would a result help you make a decision now? How would you feel about sharing it with family? What support is available if uncertainty is difficult? Counseling after testing is equally important because the laboratory wording alone may not provide a usable care plan.

Consent means understanding the choice

Testing should proceed with informed consent, usually documented in writing. Before agreeing, you should understand the purpose of the test, its expected accuracy and limitations, potential benefits and harms, possible outcomes and alternatives. You can ask questions, take time to decide or decline testing. Continuing risk assessment and appropriate care does not depend on agreeing to every offered test.

Ask who will receive the result, where it will be stored, how the sample may be used and whether research participation is a separate choice. Clarify the clinic’s process for discussing unexpected findings and sharing information with relatives. Privacy and insurance protections depend on your country, the provider and the type of insurance; obtain local advice rather than assuming the same rules apply everywhere.

Choosing the test and giving a sample

A test can look specifically for a known family variant, assess one gene more broadly or examine several genes in a panel. More genes do not always mean a more useful answer. A larger panel may find information beyond the original question or produce additional uncertain findings. The choice should fit the clinical purpose and the amount of information you want.

The sample is commonly a small blood draw, although saliva or cells collected from inside the cheek may be suitable. It is sent to a laboratory with expertise in genetic analysis. Results often take several weeks, but timing varies by test and service. Before leaving, confirm how you will receive them and whether a results appointment is already arranged.

A positive result can guide action without predicting destiny

A positive result usually means a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant has been found. These terms describe evidence that the change is associated with disease risk. They do not mean you already have cancer or that cancer is certain. The estimated risk depends on the gene, the particular variant, your age and other factors.

Possible next steps include screening earlier or more often, a different screening method, medicines that reduce selected risks or risk-reducing surgery. For example, mastectomy may be discussed for some people with high inherited breast-cancer risk; it is not the automatic response to any positive result. Benefits, harms, timing, fertility implications and personal preferences belong in a specialist discussion. Healthy habits remain worthwhile but cannot guarantee prevention or cancel an inherited risk.

A negative result has more than one meaning

If a harmful variant is already known in your family and your test specifically shows that you did not inherit it, the result is a true negative for that variant. This can be reassuring. It does not eliminate ordinary cancer risk or other risks identified through your own history or the other side of your family.

If no harmful family variant has been identified, a negative panel may be uninformative: the test did not find an explanation, but that does not establish that there is none. Some relevant genes or types of changes may not have been tested or understood. Screening should still reflect your personal and family history. A negative report is not, by itself, permission to stop recommended surveillance.

An uncertain result is not a positive diagnosis

A variant of uncertain significance, or VUS, is a change for which the available evidence cannot yet establish whether it increases disease risk. It should not alone trigger risk-reducing surgery or another major change in care. Management instead rests on established risk factors and clinical history.

A classification may change as research accumulates. Ask the testing service who tracks reclassification, how you would be contacted and whether you need to update your contact details. Keep the report. Relatives should not automatically undergo predictive testing or change care based only on your VUS; the genetics team can advise whether any specific family study would be useful.

Accuracy is different from certainty about future illness

A well-performed test can accurately identify a variant while still being unable to predict whether a particular person will develop cancer. Finding a risk factor and forecasting an individual future are different tasks. Conversely, a test with a limited scope may miss an important variant even when the laboratory correctly reports everything it was designed to examine.

Ask about the test’s coverage and limitations rather than relying on a single accuracy percentage. Consumer testing may assess selected variants or supply results without adequate interpretation. A negative consumer report should not override a concerning history, and an unexpected positive should receive appropriate clinical confirmation and counseling before treatment decisions. The most useful report is one that leads to a clear, evidence-based follow-up plan.

Potential benefits and emotional costs

An informative negative result can bring relief. A harmful finding can create an opportunity to act earlier, tailor care or help relatives understand their own choices. For someone already diagnosed with cancer, it may also influence treatment or assessment of other cancer risks. These benefits depend on what was found and whether useful follow-up is available.

The experience can also bring anxiety, uncertainty, family tension or guilt. Someone who did not inherit a familial variant may feel uncomfortable being relieved when a sibling is affected. Someone with a positive result may worry about children. Neither result is a personal failure. Blood or cheek sampling usually carries little physical risk, but the emotional and practical consequences deserve time and support. A counselor or trusted support person can help you work through them.

Discuss costs and access before proceeding

The price depends on the test’s scope, laboratory and healthcare system. Counseling, sample collection, analysis, confirmation and later specialist appointments may be billed separately. Some health plans or public services cover medically indicated testing; others have eligibility criteria, preauthorization requirements or limits. Ask for the expected personal cost rather than assuming all genetic tests receive the same coverage.

If cost would prevent you from testing, ask the clinic about supported services or financial assistance. Also ask whether a different, more focused test would answer the clinical question. Financial planning should include the possible follow-up, not just the initial laboratory bill. Avoid relying on a fixed price quoted for another country or an older testing service.

Make a follow-up plan for yourself and your family

Review the result with a clinician experienced in cancer genetics and obtain a written plan: which screening or risk-reduction options apply, who will arrange them and when the plan should be reviewed. Update the team if another relative develops cancer or new family test information emerges. Additional testing may sometimes become useful as knowledge changes, but repeating the same test routinely is not necessarily helpful.

If a harmful variant is confirmed, ask which relatives may benefit from targeted testing and whether the service can provide a family letter. Each relative should be supported in making their own decision. Testing children depends on the condition and whether the information would change childhood care; adult-onset risk does not automatically justify testing a young child. If you are considering pregnancy, request a separate, non-directive discussion of inheritance and reproductive options.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NCI and American Cancer Society guidance support history-based assessment, appropriate test selection and counseling before and after testing.

A pathogenic variant indicates increased risk, while an uninformative negative or VUS does not independently resolve clinical risk.

Sampling risk is generally small; psychological, family, financial and privacy implications remain important.

How BeMama can help

The full written-source adaptation covers the rationale, cancer types, assessment, consent, sampling, results, benefits, downsides and costs, with distinctions needed to avoid false reassurance or unnecessary intervention.

When to seek help

This is educational information. A cancer-genetics professional should interpret individual results and advise on screening, treatment or testing relatives. Specialist review and local eligibility/privacy checks remain pending before publication.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Genetic changes drive cancer, but most cancers are not explained by a single harmful inherited variant.
  • A genetics assessment considers both family lineages, your own history and what testing could change.
  • Positive, true-negative, uninformative-negative and uncertain findings require different interpretations.
  • A VUS alone should not drive major preventive decisions.
  • Consent, privacy, costs, emotional support and a results appointment are part of the testing process.

Frequently asked questions

Is cancer itself passed from a parent to a child?

No. A parent can pass on a genetic change that raises the chance of certain cancers. That is an inherited predisposition, not the transmission of a tumor or a guarantee of illness.

Does cancer on my father’s side of the family matter?

Yes. Relevant variants can come through either parental lineage. Include cancers in both men and women and on both sides when preparing a family history.

Do two relatives with breast cancer automatically mean I need a BRCA test?

They are a reason to discuss assessment. Ages at diagnosis, tumor details and existing family reports help determine whether testing is appropriate and whether a targeted or multigene test is most useful.

Why might an affected relative be tested first?

Finding a harmful variant in someone who has had cancer can give the family a specific change to test for. If no affected relative is available, testing may still be considered, but a negative result can be harder to interpret.

Does a positive result mean I must have surgery?

No. The care plan depends on the gene and your circumstances. Screening, medicines or surgery may be discussed, with benefits and harms explained. There is no single intervention for every positive result.

Can I stop screening after a negative result?

Not simply because the report is negative. Your team needs to distinguish a true negative for a known family variant from an uninformative negative and consider your remaining risk factors.

Is a variant of uncertain significance a harmful mutation?

It has not been established as harmful or harmless. It should not alone determine major treatment or prevention decisions. Ask how you will hear about any future reclassification.

Will testing during my cancer treatment tell me about inherited risk?

It depends on what was tested. Tumor profiling and germline testing answer different questions. Bring the report to your clinician so they can decide whether separate inherited-risk testing is needed.

Can I decline genetic testing after counseling?

Yes. Counseling supports an informed choice. You can ask about alternatives and how your care would be planned if you choose not to test or need more time.

Should my child be tested if I have an inherited cancer variant?

Ask a genetics specialist about that particular condition. Testing may be useful when it changes care during childhood, while testing for predominantly adult-onset risk is often deferred. A parent’s positive result does not create one rule for every child.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
